rewrites.summary:
No trans-specific statute, enforcement pattern or incident documentation exists for this province. That absence is recorded as absence of documented divergence — not as evidence of local permissiveness: the nationwide framework below governs here as in every province.

As documented nationally: a judicial package leaked in October 2025 would make conduct judged contrary to biological sex or general morality punishable by up to three years, criminalise same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies (up to four years), and bar gender-affirming care under age 25 behind a permanent-infertility assessment, with patients and providers exposed to prosecution; civil-society groups and the country's medical association protested, and an established human-rights court precedent is invoked against it. The 2025 report of the country's longest-running LGBTI monitoring body describes hostility becoming explicit state policy — 'family' directives to public institutions, the first closure of an LGBTI organisation in years, and hundreds of recorded rights violations: 6 right-to-life cases (3 hate-motivated killings), 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, 313 deprivations of liberty with 299 detention decisions, and expression violations rising from 216 to 540.

rewrites.summary:
Antioquia contains the city at the centre of the country's most alarming recent record on anti-trans killings. On 4 April 2025 in Bello, a 32-year-old trans woman, Sara Millerey González Borja, was beaten and thrown into a waterway while onlookers filmed her; she died of her injuries. She was the third LGBT person killed in Bello that year — the first two were gay men — and the case triggered vigils, protests in several cities and a presidential order to investigate, amid a national tally of 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025 alone.

The national frame around that series, as documented: more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023 (41 recorded) and eight more between February and April 2024; armed groups in at least one southern department have circulated flyers announcing 'social cleansing' against trans women, in territories where ex-rebel structures persist despite the 2016 peace agreement. The surviving record supports a lethal concentration around Antioquia's metro area — three municipal killings within four months — and documents no province-level protection machinery specific to it.

The case triggered vigils, multi-city protests and a presidential order to investigate, amid 13 trans killings nationally in the first quarter of 2025. The national frame: more than 40 trans women killed in 2023 and eight in early 2024; armed groups in one southern department circulated 'social cleansing' flyers against trans women where ex-rebel structures persist. The surviving record supports a lethal concentration around this region's metro area and documents no province-level protection machinery here.

rewrites.summary:
The region's documented contact point with trans-visitor risk is prison placement, which national law sets: under criminal-procedure code Article D248 a trans prisoner is held according to the sex on their identity documents, so trans women still marked male are placed in all-male facilities. An investigation published in January 2018 recorded exactly that near the region's principal city: Paola, shouted at and threatened by inmates during three days in a men's facility after a 2014 transfer, and — in the capital — Kara B., held under notorious conditions after a 2016 protest trial; the national detention inspector-general calls transgender detainees the group that suffers most in custody.

The inspector-general's May 2021 opinion, covering every place of deprivation of liberty in the state and built from some forty referrals since 2010, finds serious violations persisting: isolation by reason of trans status, untrained staff, and a 2016 depathologisation law never translated into prison rules. It recommends that detainees choose the sex of searching officers and of their ward, bars identity-based isolation and trans-only wings, and requires continuity of hormone and medical care — recommendations whose non-implementation is itself part of the documented picture for visitors who are detained anywhere in the state, including here.

A 2018 investigation recorded that pattern in a men's facility near this region's principal city — one transferee shouted at and threatened by inmates — and in the capital's notorious conditions for another; the national detention inspector-general calls transgender detainees the group that suffers most in custody. The inspector's 2021 opinion across all places of deprivation of liberty (~40 referrals since 2010) finds persisting serious violations — identity-based isolation, untrained staff, an unimplemented 2016 depathologisation law — and recommends detainees choose search-officer and ward sex, no trans-status isolation, and continuity of medical care.

National detention inspector-general, opinion (25 May 2021) on transgender persons in all places of deprivation of liberty (~40 referrals since 2010, plus interviews and inspections): serious violations persist; recommends detainees choose the sex of search officers and ward, no isolation for trans identity, no trans-only wings, continuing hormone and medical care; extends to intersex and non-binary people; notes the 2016 depathologisation law was never implemented in prison rules.
